8363.etyen:
Inherited from Old Norse bygsla (“to lease, let”), derived from Old Norse byggja (“to let out; lend money at interest”) with the suffixal element -sl-, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *bugjaną (“to deal, do business; buy, purchase”), of uncertain deeper origin.
The relevant “lease out” sense of byggja continued into Middle Norwegian; a 1427 document has the form bygdhi in this sense.
The underlying byggja is cognate with Old English bycgan, Old Saxon buggian, Gothic 𐌱𐌿𐌲𐌾𐌰𐌽 (bugjan) and English buy. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk bygsle and bygsla (“to lease land”).

1000107.etyen:
Internationalism, based on the name Tanzania, coined in 1964 as a blend of Tanganyika and Zanzibar, with -ia, combining the names of the two states that united that year.
The Tanganyika element is ultimately from the name of Lake Tanganyika. The lake name is probably from Swahili changanyika (“to become mixed, be mixed together”), from changanya (“to mix”), ultimately from Proto-Bantu *-cànga. The name may originally have referred to the mixing of waters. A widespread alternative interpretation connects the name with Swahili tanga (“sail”) and nyika (“wilderness, uninhabited country”), yieldin

1004459.etyen:
Probably a Danish form corresponding to gisning (“guess, conjecture”), a verbal noun of gisse (“to guess”). The word family is attested in Old Danish as gitze (“to guess”). Its deeper origin is uncertain: NAOB tentatively connects the family with a Germanic root *getan and notes semantic influence from gissen (“to guess”) and Middle Low German gissen (“to guess”). The literary verb gisne (“to guess, conjecture”) was later back-formed from this noun.
By surface analysis, gisse (“to guess”) + -ning (“verbal-noun-forming suffix”).

1004971.etyen:
From Håvard (“male given name”) + -s- (“genitive or linking element”) + son (“patronymic suffix meaning “son of””), originally a patronymic meaning “son of Håvard”.
The given name Håvard goes back to Old Norse Hávarðr, for which two Proto-Norse preforms have been reconstructed: *Hauhawarduz, literally “high guardian”, and *Haþuwarduz, literally “battle guardian”. The second element of both forms continues Proto-Germanic *warduz (“guard, guardian”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *wer- (“to heed, watch”).
Compare Icelandic Hávarðsson and Faroese Hávarðsson (“patronymics”).
